usage: Standard verb is 따다 (to earn), not 받다.
Common compound; the test you take to earn it.
Put the field before 자격증 to specify the type (요리 자격증, 컴퓨터 자격증, etc.).
Useful when listing qualifications on a resume or to an employer.
examples: 이직하려고 자격증을 하나 더 따고 있어요.
I'm getting one more certificate to change jobs.
이직하다 = change jobs; very common motivation for adults studying.
그 회사는 토익 점수보다 자격증을 더 봐요.
That company looks at certificates more than TOEIC scores.
보다 here means 'to consider/value' when evaluating applicants.
주말마다 자격증 학원에 다녀요.
I go to a certification academy every weekend.
다니다 = to attend regularly; natural for ongoing classes.
nuance: 자격증 is the umbrella word for any official qualification certificate, from cooking to computing to driving. Adults in Korea constantly collect 자격증 to boost their resume, so it comes up in any conversation about career or self-improvement. Pair it with 따다 (earn) rather than 사다 or 받다.
mistakes: Saying 자격증을 사다 — you earn (따다) a certificate, you don't 'buy' it.
Confusing 자격증 (qualification) with 증명서 (proof document like a transcript).

usage: 듣다 (to listen) is the standard verb for any lecture, online or not.
결제 = payment; these courses are usually paid subscriptions.
Star 인강 강사 can be celebrities among students.
Use -으로 to mark the method of studying.
examples: 요즘은 학원 안 가고 인강으로 공부해요.
These days I study with online lectures instead of going to an academy.
Shows the common trade-off between in-person 학원 and 인강.
인강은 배속으로 들으면 시간이 절약돼요.
If you watch lectures at faster speed, you save time.
배속 = playback speed; a very real study habit in Korea.
그 인강 진짜 잘 가르쳐서 추천해요.
That online lecture teaches really well, so I recommend it.
잘 가르치다 = teaches well; natural praise for a lecturer.
nuance: 인강 is a contraction of 인터넷 강의 (internet lecture) and is everyday slang, not formal vocabulary. It refers specifically to pre-recorded video courses you stream, hugely popular for exam prep and self-study. Use 듣다 with it, the same verb you'd use for any 강의.
mistakes: Writing 인강의 — the slang is just 인강; the full form 인터넷 강의 keeps 강의.
Using 보다 exclusively — Koreans say 인강을 듣다 (listen) even though it's video.

usage: 받다 when you're the student getting taught.
하다 when you're the tutor; common student part-time job.
선생님 is the polite way to refer to your tutor.
examples: 대학생 때 수학 과외를 해서 용돈을 벌었어요.
I earned pocket money tutoring math in college.
Classic Korean student side job; 용돈 = pocket money.
아이한테 과외를 시킬까 고민 중이에요.
I'm debating whether to get my kid private tutoring.
시키다 = to make/arrange for someone; parents 'arrange' 과외.
그룹 과외라서 학원보다 조금 싸요.
It's group tutoring, so it's a bit cheaper than an academy.
그룹 과외 = small-group tutoring, a middle option.
nuance: 과외 means private, usually one-on-one tutoring at home, distinct from 학원 (academy classes) and 인강 (online lectures). Students 하다 it as a job; learners 받다 it. Parents 시키다 it for their children. It carries a slightly premium, personalized nuance compared to group classes.
mistakes: Mixing up 받다 and 하다 — the student receives (받다), the tutor does (하다).
Assuming 과외 always means kids — adults also get 과외 for languages or instruments.

usage: 보다 is the standard verb for sitting an exam.
A national event; flights pause during the listening test.
Determines which universities a student can apply to.
A landmark phrase marking the start of freedom for seniors.
examples: 수능 날에는 비행기도 잠깐 멈춰요.
On CSAT day, even planes pause briefly.
True fact about the English listening section; great cultural note.
조카가 올해 수능을 봐서 온 가족이 긴장했어요.
My niece took the CSAT this year, so the whole family was nervous.
Shows how family-wide the event feels.
수능 끝났으니까 이제 좀 놀아도 돼요.
The CSAT is over, so now you can relax a bit.
Captures the post-exam relief tone.
nuance: 수능 (short for 대학수학능력시험) is the single national university entrance exam taken once a year in November, and it is a massive cultural event in Korea. As a resident you'll notice altered traffic, hushed neighborhoods, and even delayed flights on 수능 날. Use 보다 (to take/sit) with it.
mistakes: Saying 수능을 하다 — exams take 보다, not 하다.
Treating it as a generic 'final exam' — 수능 is specifically the once-a-year national college entrance test.

usage: 보다 is the verb for sitting any test.
to work through a practice test
풀다 (to solve) for actually doing the problems.
Mock exams are scheduled monthly and named by month.
examples: 모의고사 보고 나서 약점을 분석했어요.
After the mock exam, I analyzed my weak points.
약점 분석 = weakness analysis, standard study routine.
이번 모의고사는 좀 어렵게 나왔어요.
This mock exam came out a bit hard.
나오다 = to come out; natural for describing how a test turned out.
모의고사 점수랑 실제 점수가 비슷했어요.
My mock-exam score and actual score were similar.
Common reassurance that mocks predict real results.
nuance: 모의고사 is a practice exam designed to simulate the real thing, especially for 수능. Students take them repeatedly to gauge progress and manage exam anxiety. Use 보다 to sit it and 풀다 to refer to working through the questions. The term applies to any standardized mock, not only college tests.
mistakes: Confusing 모의고사 with 중간고사 (midterm) — 모의고사 is a rehearsal, not a graded school exam.
Saying 모의고사를 하다 instead of 보다.

usage: to prepare for the essay exam
준비하다 = to prepare; these tests need dedicated practice.
Specialized academies exist just for 논술.
전형 = admissions method; one route into university.
examples: 논술은 답이 하나가 아니라서 더 어려워요.
Essay exams are harder because there's no single answer.
Captures the open-ended nature of 논술.
대학 논술 준비하느라 글쓰기 연습을 많이 했어요.
I practiced a lot of writing to prepare for the university essay exam.
글쓰기 = writing practice; the core skill for 논술.
논술 전형으로 대학에 합격했어요.
I got into university through the essay-based track.
Shows 논술 전형 as an admissions pathway.
nuance: 논술 refers to argumentative essay exams that test logical reasoning and writing, used as one university-admissions route alongside grades and the 수능. Unlike multiple-choice tests, 논술 has no single correct answer, which makes dedicated 논술 academies a thing. The word literally combines 논 (argue) and 술 (state).
mistakes: Confusing 논술 (argumentative essay) with 작문/에세이 (general composition).
Assuming any writing test is 논술 — it specifically means structured, argument-based exams.

usage: 받다 when the degree is conferred to you.
따다 emphasizes the effort of obtaining it.
석사 = master's; 학사 = bachelor's; 박사 = doctorate.
examples: 한국에서 석사 학위를 따려고 유학 왔어요.
I came to study abroad to earn a master's degree in Korea.
유학 오다 = to come study abroad; relevant for resident learners.
박사 학위까지 받으려면 시간이 오래 걸려요.
It takes a long time to get all the way to a doctorate.
Shows degree hierarchy and the long timeline.
그 일은 관련 학위가 있어야 지원할 수 있어요.
You need a related degree to apply for that job.
Practical for job-hunting conversations.
nuance: 학위 is your formal academic degree: 학사 (bachelor's), 석사 (master's), or 박사 (doctorate). Use 받다 (be conferred) or 따다 (earn) with it, and pair it with 과정 to talk about the program itself. It matters in Korea for both employment and visa-status conversations.
mistakes: Confusing 학위 (degree) with 학력 (level of education attained, e.g., high-school graduate).
Saying 학위를 하다 — use 받다 or 따다.

usage: The whole multi-year process, not a single test.
Academies focused on getting students into university.
대학 입시 is the most common collocation.
to go through the admissions process
치르다 = to undergo (a formal process or exam).
examples: 한국 입시는 경쟁이 정말 치열해요.
Korean college admissions are really fiercely competitive.
치열하다 = fierce; the defining word for 입시.
입시 때문에 고등학생들이 스트레스를 많이 받아요.
High schoolers get a lot of stress because of admissions.
Common social-commentary context.
입시 설명회에 부모님들이 많이 오셨어요.
Many parents came to the admissions briefing.
설명회 = info session; parents are deeply involved.
nuance: 입시 refers to the entire entrance-examination and admissions process, especially the high-stakes race into university, rather than one exam. It carries strong connotations of intense competition and is a constant topic in Korean society and media. You'll hear it paired with 준비, 학원, and 경쟁.
mistakes: Equating 입시 with a single test — it's the whole admissions process including 수능, 논술, and interviews.
Confusing 입시 (entering school) with 취업 (entering the workforce).

usage: 부르다 = to call; what the teacher does at class start.
인정 = recognition; e.g., a sick day still counted.
examples: 출석을 다 채워야 학점을 받을 수 있어요.
You have to complete all attendance to get credit.
채우다 = to fill/meet; common at university.
교수님이 매 수업마다 출석을 불러요.
The professor calls roll every single class.
매 수업마다 = every class; 부르다 for roll call.
출석만 잘해도 점수가 올라가요.
Just attending well alone raises your score.
Reflects how attendance often counts toward grades.
nuance: 출석 means being present and is the noun behind everyday phrases like 출석 체크 and 출석을 부르다. In Korean universities and academies, 출석 frequently counts directly toward your grade, so it's a practical word. The opposite is 결석 (absence).
mistakes: Confusing 출석 (attendance at class) with 출근 (attendance at work).
Saying 출석하다 when you mean 'be present at an event' — for events use 참석하다.

usage: 하다 is the verb; the whole word acts as a noun.
Half-joking phrase about being good at last-minute prep.
examples: 어제 밤새 벼락치기 했더니 너무 피곤해요.
I crammed all night yesterday, so I'm exhausted.
밤새다 = stay up all night; classic cramming scenario.
벼락치기로는 좋은 점수 받기 힘들어요.
It's hard to get a good score by cramming.
Common advice against last-minute studying.
시험이 내일인데 또 벼락치기야.
The exam is tomorrow and it's cramming again.
Casual -야 ending; relatable student grumble.
nuance: 벼락치기 literally means 'lightning strike' and refers to frantic last-minute studying right before a test. It's casual, everyday vocabulary that any student or recent grad will recognize and use about themselves with a rueful tone. Combine with 하다 or use -로 to mark it as your study method.
mistakes: Treating 벼락치기 as formal — it's colloquial; avoid it in academic writing.
Saying 벼락치기를 보다 — you 하다 cramming, you don't 'see' it.

usage: Very common about tough exam questions.
ㅂ-irregular: 까다롭다 becomes 까다로운 before a noun.
Used for hard-to-meet conditions, e.g., scholarships.
굴다 = to behave a certain way.
examples: 이번 시험은 문제가 너무 까다로웠어요.
This exam's questions were so tricky.
까다로웠어요 shows the ㅂ-irregular past tense.
그 교수님은 채점이 까다로워서 학점 받기 어려워요.
That professor grades strictly, so it's hard to get a good grade.
채점 = grading; pairs naturally with 까다롭다.
장학금 신청 조건이 생각보다 까다로워요.
The scholarship application requirements are pickier than expected.
Practical for resident learners applying for aid.
nuance: 까다롭다 describes something tricky and hard to satisfy, whether exam questions, requirements, or a fussy person. It's a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so it conjugates to 까다로워요 and 까다로운. In a study context it's the go-to word for difficult, finicky test questions or strict graders.
mistakes: Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular — it's 까다로워요, never 까다롭아요.
Using it to mean simply 'difficult' — 어렵다 is plain hard; 까다롭다 adds finicky/fussy nuance.

usage: The single most common pairing in a study context.
examples: 벼락치기보다 꾸준히 공부하는 게 나아요.
Studying steadily is better than cramming.
Direct contrast with 벼락치기 above.
한국어를 꾸준히 하면 금방 늘어요.
If you keep at Korean steadily, you improve quickly.
Encouraging line aimed right at the learner.
그 학생은 꾸준히 출석해서 성적이 올랐어요.
That student attended consistently, so their grades rose.
Ties together 출석 and steady effort.
nuance: 꾸준히 means doing something steadily and consistently over time without giving up, and it's the praise word Koreans use for sustainable effort. In any study or self-improvement talk it's the natural opposite of cramming or quitting. It modifies verbs like 공부하다, 연습하다, and 하다.
mistakes: Confusing 꾸준히 (consistently over time) with 열심히 (hard, with intensity) — you can be 열심히 once but 꾸준히 means ongoing.
Using it as an adjective — it's an adverb; the adjective form is 꾸준하다.
